s1.syndrome_frame: Acute orbital syndrome with pain, vision loss, and extraocular movement limitation
salient_findings: Diffuse limitation in extraocular movements in the left eye
Left-sided lacrimal sac abscess with postseptal fat stranding
key_facts: History of epiphora without prior dacryocystitis
Postseptal fat stranding largely limited to the extraconal space
Globe compression due to increased abscess size
Acute injury to the entire orbital segment of the left optic nerve
Initial cultures isolated gram-positive cocci in chains, later identified as pan-susceptible Streptococcus pyogenes

raw.syndrome_frame: Acute orbital syndrome with pain, vision loss, and extraocular movement limitation
salient_findings: Diffuse limitation in extraocular movements in the left eye
Left-sided lacrimal sac abscess with postseptal fat stranding
key_facts: History of epiphora without prior dacryocystitis
Postseptal fat stranding largely limited to the extraconal space
Globe compression due to increased abscess size
Acute injury to the entire orbital segment of the left optic nerve
Initial cultures isolated gram-positive cocci in chains, later identified as pan-susceptible Streptococcus pyogenes

raw.rationale: The presence of a left-sided lacrimal sac abscess with postseptal fat stranding and globe compression due to increased abscess size, as seen on imaging studies, strongly supports the diagnosis of an orbital abscess. The acute injury to the orbital segment of the left optic nerve and the significant decrease in visual acuity (20/400 OS) are also consistent with complications arising from an orbital abscess.

rejected.label: Lacrimal sac abscess
rejected.why: While a lacrimal sac abscess is present, the extent of the infection and involvement of the orbit suggests a more comprehensive diagnosis of orbital abscess is more appropriate.

rejected.label: Streptococcal orbital infection
rejected.why: Although Streptococcus pyogenes was isolated, the diagnosis of an orbital abscess encompasses the infection and its complications more accurately than specifying the causative organism alone.

rejected.label: Orbital cellulitis
rejected.why: Orbital cellulitis typically refers to an infection of the orbital tissues without a defined abscess, which does not align with the imaging findings of an abscess in this case.

rejected.label: Orbital apex syndrome
rejected.why: While the patient has significant orbital involvement, the findings do not specifically indicate the classic triad of orbital apex syndrome (ophthalmoplegia, ptosis, and decreased vision), and the primary issue appears to be an abscess rather than a syndrome affecting the orbital apex.
